articles.title: Galaxies in a cosmic house of mirrors
articles.description:
Image:
			
This NASA/ESA/CSA James Webb Space Telescope Picture of the Month features galaxies in great detail that have been warped and multiplied like they’ve stepped into a house of mirrors. The brilliant golden galaxies splashed across this image belong to a galaxy cluster called MACS J0454.1-0300. The orange galaxies concentrated on one side of the cluster are not actually part of the cluster and are much farther away from us.
MACS J0454.1-0300 is itself immensely distant: the light from these galaxies has been travelling to us for so long that we’re seeing the cluster as it was when the Universe was about 8 billion years old. While this galaxy cluster is a valuable scientific target in its own right, the real stars of this image are the galaxies that appear warped and stretched, like a painting that has been smeared by a giant hand.
The way these galaxies look is the result of gravitational lensing, in which the enormous mass of a foreground object such as a galaxy cluster bends and magnifies the light from a more distant object in the background. Gravitational lensing allows astronomers to observe galaxies, star clusters and even individual stars that are too far away for our telescopes to see under normal conditions. While the large, orange galaxies appear obviously distorted, look carefully at some of the small reddish background galaxies throughout this picture: even at the very edges of the frame, there are galaxies whose images have been bent into tiny arcs by MACS J0454.1-0300’s gravity.
The gravitationally lensed areas show multiple images of galaxies from when the Universe was young: a group of galaxies 2 billion years after the Big Bang, and a single galaxy just 800 million years old after the Big Bang. The galaxy group appears to be going through a merger, resulting in an enormous burst of star formation.
Astronomers have also identified individual bright ‘knots’ within the gravitationally lensed areas, corresponding to regions as small as 5 light-years across. These tiny clumps appear magnified by a factor of more than 300, in some cases.
A NASA/ESA Hubble Space Telescope image of this same cluster was released in 2014. Take a moment to compare the two images; the difference between them is dramatic. The new Webb image reveals hundreds of galaxies missing from the earlier image. These galaxies were there all along, but Webb is much more sensitive to their much redder light.
The data behind this image come from two observing programmes (#5058, PI: Furtak; #6882, PI: Fujimoto) that leverage the ability of massive galaxy clusters to bring distant objects into view.
[Image Description: A massive galaxy cluster, made of many golden elliptical galaxies with the largest, brightest one in the centre. Heavily distorted orange galaxies appear all around the cluster, the largest concentrated in a large arc around the cluster's centre; these are images of very distant galaxies, created by gravitational lensing. A few galaxies are large and bluish-white in colour; bright, nearby stars are the same colour.]
Release on esawebb.org
articles.summary: The James Webb Space Telescope has captured an extraordinary image of gravitationally lensed galaxies acting as a cosmic magnifying glass, revealing unprecedented detail about distant galactic structures. This phenomenon showcases the universe's most powerful natural telescopes.

articles.title: Astronomer leads global team on NASA mission to create unprecedented view of the early universe
articles.description: A University of Missouri astronomer is leading a team of 130 researchers from 62 institutions—including NASA, the California Institute of Technology, Princeton University and Harvard University—on an ambitious mission to capture an unprecedented view of the early universe.
articles.source: Space News - Space, Astronomy, Space Exploration
articles.summary: A University of Missouri astronomer leads an international team of 130 researchers from 62 institutions on a groundbreaking NASA mission to capture an unprecedented view of the early universe. This landmark collaboration promises revolutionary insights into the cosmos's distant past.

articles.title: Astronomers discover a strange universal rule behind black hole eruptions
articles.description: Scientists have discovered that black holes of vastly different sizes appear to launch powerful jets according to the same universal rule. The breakthrough could explain why some black holes suddenly erupt years after devouring a star and help astronomers predict when these spectacular outbursts will happen.
articles.summary: Astronomers have discovered a universal rule governing how black holes of vastly different sizes launch powerful jets into space. This groundbreaking finding reveals fundamental connections in the most extreme objects in the universe.

articles.title: James Webb reveals a massive cosmic structure that challenges our understanding of the Universe
articles.description: NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope has revealed an ancient galaxy cluster with an unexpectedly dense concentration of dark matter, challenging theories about how the universe developed. The discovery also uncovered a surprising connection between scattered starlight and invisible dark matter that could transform how astronomers study the early cosmos.
articles.summary: NASA's James Webb Space Telescope has discovered an ancient, unexpectedly dense galaxy cluster that challenges current cosmological models. This remarkable finding offers new insights into the universe's earliest epochs and structure formation.

articles.title: IceCube, high-energy neutrinos, and Francis Halzen win 2026’s Physics Nobel
articles.description:
Back in 1988, Francis Halzen had what he called a “cute idea.” His vision grew into the IceCube observatory, and earns the 2026 Nobel…
Continue reading on Starts With A Bang! »
articles.summary: Francis Halzen and the IceCube observatory win the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physics for groundbreaking discoveries in high-energy neutrino astronomy.

articles.title: Mars moon lander set to launch on 19 October
articles.description:
The Martian Moons eXploration (MMX) mission is set to launch into space on a H3 rocket from the Tanegashima Space Center at 04:41 JST on 20 October 2026 (20:41 BST / 21:41 CEST on 19 October 2026). MMX will be the first mission to collect a sample from Mars’s moon Phobos and bring it back to Earth. 
MMX is led by the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA), in collaboration with the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA), the French space agency (CNES), the German Aerospace Center (DLR) and the European Space Agency (ESA).
articles.summary: The Martian Moons eXploration (MMX) mission is preparing to launch on October 19 aboard Japan's H3 rocket to study Mars's mysterious moons. This landmark mission will provide unprecedented insights into the formation and composition of Phobos and Deimos.

articles.title: Solar Orbiter tracks origin of mysterious magnetic switchbacks
articles.description: The European Space Agency-led Solar Orbiter spacecraft has flown through an S-shaped kink known as a ‘switchback’ in the solar wind’s magnetic field. By fingerprinting the elusive particles within the switchback, Solar Orbiter has traced its origin back to the Sun’s surface and revealed more about solar magnetism – the unruly instigator of dangerous solar storms.
articles.summary: The ESA's Solar Orbiter has made groundbreaking observations of magnetic switchbacks—S-shaped kinks in the solar wind that challenge our understanding of the Sun's magnetic field. This discovery helps scientists unravel the mysteries of solar dynamics and space weather.

articles.title: Webb captures commotion from nebula’s stellar jets
articles.description:
Image:
			Webb captures commotion from nebula’s stellar jets
articles.summary: The James Webb Space Telescope has captured stunning images of stellar jets erupting from a nebula, revealing the dynamic processes of star formation. These observations showcase the violent and beautiful chaos at the birthplaces of stars.

articles.title: Science begins for Smile
articles.description: On 23 September, the European-Chinese Smile mission was declared ready to start revealing how Earth responds to the wind of charged particles from the Sun. This follows a busy in-space commissioning period since the spacecraft launched on 19 May and reached its target orbit for science operations on 20 June.
articles.summary: The European-Chinese Smile mission was declared ready on September 23 to begin its groundbreaking investigation of how Earth's magnetosphere responds to solar wind. This collaborative mission will revolutionize our understanding of space weather interactions.

articles.title: In the Search for Exoplanets, Some Failures Are A Success
articles.description: Astronomers used decades of archival data and new radial velocity measurements to search for exoplanets around a neaby binary star, 70 Oph AB. They didn't find any, which can seem like a failure. But in this case, their work only ruled out large, Jupiter-mass planets at certain distances. There could still be Earth-sized planets there, and their precise findings will only fuel a deeper search with more powerful telescopes.
articles.summary: Astronomers have successfully identified exoplanets by analyzing decades of archival radial velocity data, demonstrating that careful reanalysis of existing observations can yield remarkable discoveries. This approach reveals new worlds hiding in previously collected scientific records.

articles.title: The Flavor of Neutrinos Could Determine How a Large Star Dies
articles.description: Neutrinos come in three different flavors. A new study finds that neutrino flavor could play a significant role in whether a dying star becomes a supernova or collapses directly into a black hole.
articles.summary: New research reveals that the three different flavors of neutrinos play a crucial role in determining how massive stars reach the end of their lives. This discovery deepens our understanding of stellar physics and the fundamental forces governing stellar death.

articles.title: A Distant Supercluster of Galaxies Points To Self-Interacting Dark Matter
articles.description: The El Gordo supercluster is unusually large given its distance. How could such a large galaxy cluster form so quickly? The answer could be that dark matter is self-interacting in an interesting two-state way.
articles.summary: The El Gordo supercluster's unusual size and early formation provide compelling evidence for self-interacting dark matter, challenging our understanding of cosmic structure formation. This discovery offers new insights into the nature of dark matter and galaxy cluster evolution.

articles.title: Host Stars Shape Their Planetary Systems Into Two Families
articles.description: New research draws a link between a host star and the characteristics of its planetary system. Higher mass stars create one family of systems, while lower mass stars create another. These results provide a new, more detailed template for understanding exoplanet systems.
articles.summary: New research demonstrates that a host star's mass fundamentally shapes the characteristics and organization of its planetary system, revealing an elegant connection between stellar properties and planetary architecture. This finding illuminates how diverse planetary systems form around different types of stars.

articles.title: Plants shift gene activity within minutes of entering spaceflight, experiment reveals
articles.description: Plants begin responding to spaceflight almost immediately after leaving Earth, according to a new University of Florida study that captured the earliest stages of biological adaptation during a commercial suborbital mission. Published in the journal npj Microgravity, the study reports the results of an experiment conducted by a UF astronaut during Blue Origin's New Shepard NS-26 flight on Aug. 29, 2024.
articles.source: Space News - Space, Astronomy, Space Exploration
articles.summary: A University of Florida experiment reveals that plants begin responding to spaceflight within minutes of launch, demonstrating remarkable biological adaptability. This discovery opens exciting possibilities for growing food and studying life in space.

articles.title: New 3D model reveals how shadows reshape chemistry in stellar nurseries
articles.description: How do young stars reshape the clouds from which they are born? A new high-resolution 3D model developed by an international team led by Dr Brandt Gaches from the University of Duisburg-Essen shows how the uneven structure of stellar nurseries creates shadows that alter their chemistry and influence the infrared emission observed by the James Webb Space Telescope. The model has now been published in Astronomy & Astrophysics.
articles.source: Space News - Space, Astronomy, Space Exploration
articles.summary: An international team has created a high-resolution 3D model revealing how young stars reshape the clouds around them through shadow effects. This breakthrough advances our understanding of stellar formation and cosmic chemistry.

articles.title: First comprehensive Mars soil classification offers framework for exploration and future farming
articles.description: A Ph.D. student at the University of Sydney has produced the first comprehensive classification system and map of Martian soils, creating a new framework that could help scientists compare landscapes across the Red Planet and identify promising locations for future exploration, habitation and food production.
articles.source: Space News - Space, Astronomy, Space Exploration
articles.summary: A University of Sydney researcher has developed the first comprehensive classification system and map of Martian soil types. This framework promises to enhance exploration strategies and support future agricultural endeavors on Mars.

articles.title: Forecasting air drag with deep learning helps predict when uncontrolled satellites and rocket stages fall to Earth
articles.description: On May 10, 2025, a spacecraft built in the Soviet Union to land on Venus came home. Launched in 1972, Cosmos-482 was stranded by a failed upper stage of its rocket and circled Earth for 53 years. In its last days, several space agencies and research groups forecasted when it would fall, and therefore where. Roscosmos later reported that it came down in the Indian Ocean, west of Jakarta.
articles.source: Space News - Space, Astronomy, Space Exploration
articles.summary: Deep learning technology is revolutionizing predictions of atmospheric drag on satellites and rocket stages, enabling better forecasting of orbital decay. This advancement enhances space situational awareness and safety for future missions.

articles.title: Scientists may have finally solved the mystery of the Moon’s two faces
articles.description: Scientists may have solved a long-standing mystery about why the Moon’s two sides are so different, using samples collected from its farside for the first time. Their findings suggest that uneven heating from Earth's gravitational pull drove enormous flows of ancient magma, creating the dramatically different lunar landscapes we see today.
articles.summary: Scientists have solved a long-standing mystery about the Moon's two dramatically different faces using lunar samples from recent missions. This breakthrough deepens our understanding of the Moon's fascinating geological history.

articles.title: A planet 320 light-years away confirms what scientists long suspected
articles.description: Astronomers have discovered that a scorching-hot planet 320 light-years away shares a striking chemical similarity with its host star, providing the first direct evidence for a fundamental assumption about planet formation. The breakthrough could help scientists predict what distant rocky planets are made of and identify worlds with conditions favorable for life.
articles.summary: Astronomers have confirmed that a scorching-hot exoplanet 320 light-years away possesses striking chemical similarities to planets in our solar system. This discovery reveals intriguing universal patterns in planetary composition across the cosmos.

articles.title: Scientists make stunning discovery that could help explain why life exists
articles.description: Scientists have discovered that the universe's fundamental physical constants may be finely balanced to make life possible. Even tiny changes to these constants could make liquids too thick or too thin for essential biological processes, potentially preventing life as we know it. Surprisingly, these life-friendly conditions existed billions of years before living cells appeared. The findings raise intriguing questions about why the laws of physics seem so well suited to life.
articles.summary: Scientists have discovered compelling evidence that the universe's fundamental physical constants are finely tuned to enable life. This stunning finding illuminates the remarkable balance underlying our existence.

articles.title: NASA astronauts splash down after 100 million miles in space
articles.description: NASA’s SpaceX Crew-12 astronauts have returned to Earth after 237 days in space, traveling more than 100 million miles and completing over 3,792 orbits while conducting research to prepare for future missions to the Moon and Mars. The mission also made history with record-setting spacewalk achievements and experiments that could transform medicine both in space and on Earth.
articles.summary: NASA's SpaceX Crew-12 astronauts have triumphantly returned to Earth after 237 days in orbit, completing a journey of over 100 million miles. This successful mission marks another milestone in humanity's expanding presence in space.

articles.title: Scientists find 'gemstones' in atmosphere of bizarre, scorching-hot 'marshmallow' exoplanet
articles.description: Using data from the James Webb Space Telescope, astronomers have unravelled some of the secrets of a bizarre, blisteringly hot exoplanet that has the consistency of marshmallow.
articles.summary: Using the James Webb Space Telescope, astronomers discovered gemstone-like atmospheric compositions on a bizarre, scorching-hot marshmallow exoplanet, revealing new insights into exotic worlds.

articles.title: Physics Nobel highlights Antarctica’s role in exploring the cosmos
articles.description: For more than a century, scientists have treated Antarctica’s environments as windows into worlds beyond Earth.
articles.summary: Antarctica's unique environment serves as an invaluable observatory for cosmic exploration, with over a century of scientific discoveries emerging from this remote continent. Recent physics recognition highlights how polar research continues to unlock mysteries of the universe.

articles.title: À 2 200 °C en rentrée terrestre, le bouclier d’Orion séparait les astronautes d’Artémis II de la désintégration. Il n’a eu que 9 zones abîmées, contre 103 lors d’Artémis I
articles.description: La NASA a publié son analyse détaillée du bouclier thermique d'Orion après la mission Artémis II. Elle y relève neuf zones de perte de matière, contre 103 après le vol inhabité d'Artémis I en 2022.
articles.summary: NASA's detailed analysis of the Orion heat shield from Artemis II reveals remarkable durability, with only 9 damaged zones compared to 103 during Artemis I, demonstrating significant engineering improvements. The shield successfully protected astronauts through re-entry at 2,200°C.

articles.title: La NASA dévoile les données scientifiques d’Artemis II : un pactole impressionnant de 996 images et de plus de 800 Go de données
articles.description: Avec les images impressionnantes qu'ils ont capturées depuis la capsule Orion, les quatre astronautes de l'équipage d'Artemis II n'ont pas fait le voyage pour rien. Mais ce n'est qu'une petite partie du pactole, que la NASA a mis en accès libre.
articles.summary: NASA releases an impressive scientific dataset from Artemis II containing 996 stunning images and over 800 gigabytes of data captured by the four-member crew from the Orion capsule. This wealth of information advances lunar exploration and scientific discovery.

articles.title: Mars’s oddest cloud may be even odder than we thought
articles.description: Scientists using the European Space Agency's Mars Express, in combination with a state-of-the-art meteorological model of the Red Planet, have found that there may be some very exotic physics behind Mars’s most curious cloud.
articles.summary: Using ESA's Mars Express and advanced meteorological modeling, scientists have discovered that Mars's enigmatic cloud formations are even more complex and fascinating than previously believed. This research deepens our understanding of Martian atmospheric phenomena.

articles.title: A galaxy spinning out of sync
articles.description:
Image:
			
Though the spiral galaxy in this new image by the NASA/ESA Hubble Space Telescope seems serene, it hides a chaotic secret. This galaxy is NGC 4698, and it lies about 55 million light-years away in the constellation Virgo. It’s one of over one thousand galaxies in the Virgo Cluster, the nearest large cluster of galaxies bound together by gravity.
As a spiral galaxy similar to our own Milky Way galaxy, NGC 4698 has spiral arms that curl around within a thin disc of stars, gas and dust. Its centre is dominated by a galactic bulge.
The diffuse off-white glow of the galaxy’s bulge comes from stars smaller, older, and cooler than the massive blue stars that dot the galaxy’s outer disc. These tightly packed stars orbit a supermassive black hole containing millions of times the Sun’s mass. Scientists have found signs that this black hole is actively growing, drawing gas inward with its gravitational pull.
With a flat, starry disc and diffusely glowing centre, NGC 4698 looks a lot like a typical spiral galaxy — but this galaxy is far from normal. NGC 4698 is one of only a few known spiral galaxies with a bulge that extends out from the disc at a right angle. The elongation is faintly visible in this Hubble image, which shows the ghostly glow of the starry bulge peeking above and below the dusty disc. What’s more, the stars and gas nearest the galaxy’s centre rotate perpendicular to the rest of the disc.
What could cause a galaxy to be so out of sync? Astronomers have found that the culprit likely lies outside the galaxy. If NGC 4698 funneled in gas from an outside source, the newly collected gas could have formed a disc of gas and stars in the galaxy’s centre, at an angle relative to the rest of the disc. Some observations suggest that this galaxy once experienced a minor galactic merger, as evidenced by a short ‘tail’ of hydrogen streaming from one side of the galaxy.
The data used to create this image come from an observing programme (#18103; PI: Thilker) focusing on galaxies in the Virgo Cluster.
[Image Description: A spiral galaxy viewed at an angle, with a bright central bulge and winding spiral arms. The arms form a ring around the galaxy, without appearing to reach its centre. Prominent red-brown dust lanes weave through the arms, which are also dotted with bright blue and reddish regions of star formation. The galaxy is set against a dark background scattered with stars and faint distant galaxies.]
Release on esawebb.org
articles.summary: The Hubble Space Telescope has imaged a spiral galaxy with unexpected internal dynamics, revealing that not all cosmic structures follow conventional expectations. This discovery adds to our understanding of galactic complexity and evolution.

articles.title: Enigmatic Mercury Will Remain A Puzzle Until Someone Sends A Lander
articles.description: Despite the upcoming Bepi Colombo visit to Mercury, we need a lander mission to fully understand our solar system’s innermost planet.
articles.summary: While the upcoming Bepi Colombo flyby of Mercury will provide valuable data, scientists recognize that a dedicated lander mission is essential for fully understanding the solar system's innermost planet. This highlights the exciting future exploration possibilities for Mercury.

articles.title: A Radio Phoenix Beyond the Zone of Avoidance
articles.description: Years ago, astronomers spotted a strange radio formation beyond the Zone of Avoidance. The formation resembles a treble clef, a symbol in musical notation, and the nickname has stuck. Determining what created it has been difficult, but new research has revealed that the Treble Clef is a radio phoenix.
articles.summary: Astronomers have discovered a remarkable radio formation beyond the Zone of Avoidance that resembles a musical treble clef, adding to the cosmic wonders hiding in regions historically difficult to observe. This unique finding showcases the universe's unexpected beauty.

articles.title: Scientists Detect Rare Type of Wood Alcohol in Space
articles.description: As part of the ALMA COMPASS Large program, an international research team has detected a rare form of methanol in space for the first time.
articles.summary: An international research team using ALMA has detected a rare form of methanol in space, expanding our knowledge of complex organic molecules in the cosmos. This discovery reveals the rich chemistry occurring throughout the universe.
